newsitem.title: UK: Gold jewellery demand seen on a steady growth path.
newsitem.headline: Gold jewellery demand seen on a steady growth path.

text.p: Jewellery demand will continue to grow in the next decade in line with an expanding global economy but a repeat of the 1980s boom is unlikely, precious metals analyst Tony Warwick-Ching of CRU International said.

"For the market as a whole the 1980s and early 90s could prove to have been a golden age for jewellery. The next ten years are likely to be tougher," Warwick-Ching noted in a speech prepared for a gold conference in Dubai on Saturday.
Some developing markets would be stimulated by liberalisation, but many others would no longer enjoy the unique combination of liberalisation and cheaper bullion.
The two "dynamos" which helped power jewellery demand in the past two decades might be absent in the future, he said.
"Liberalisation is increasingly a spent force for good...and could cause problems by opening up other avenues for investment and consumer spending," Warwick-Ching said.

Dwindling demand for gold as an asset or investment has cast a critical role for the jewellery industry. Analysts say it will have to absorb more of the available stocks just to keep the market steady, even if mine ouput remains steady.

"In terms of its end-markets...the gold industry is fast approaching the status of a one-club golfer," said Warwick-Ching. Jewellery took up 80 percent of all gold manufactures, although electronics and decorative uses were also buoyant.
But despite the sector's growth, in most developing countries demand had barely kept pace with the expansion in world GDP and the trend was slowing down.
In China, for instance, jewellery would have to fight harder for the consumer dollar as the diversity of retail and financial products grew with waves of liberalisation.
Jewellery demand would be strongest in countries where gold liberalisation is accompanied by high and rapidly rising incomes but "such places are now few and far between".
India was one exception as it responded well to lower prices and a more gradual approach to liberalisation, while Dubai could this year rival the record import of 580 tonnes in 1968.
In Japan, gold offtake seemed to have stopped growing seven years ago amid a heightened sensitivity to price at a low level, a situation not helped by the yen's weakness.
